title: Dutch consumer group v. Meta: Amsterdam court heard the Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses case on November 26
subtitle: Consumentenbond, Offlimits and The Firewall asked a Dutch judge to force Meta to retool the glasses' default behavior or pull them from sale, citing GDPR obligations the groups say Meta's always-on camera design cannot meet.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Amsterdam District Court heard three coordinated Dutch cases against Meta on November 26 over the Ray-Ban Meta camera glasses. Consumentenbond, the country's largest consumer association, asked the court to order Meta to change the glasses and their default settings so that recording complies with EU data protection law — and only to ban Dutch sales if Meta argues compliance is impossible. The group also asked for a medical-necessity exception for blind and partially sighted users. Offlimits, which represents people targeted by image-based abuse, asked for the glasses to be removed from Dutch retail. The Firewall, a digital-rights NGO, joined the proceedings alongside them.

The groups' lawyers argue that Meta bears direct GDPR liability because footage captured by the glasses routes through Meta's servers for AI processing, and that images and sound are special categories of personal data under Dutch implementation of the regulation. Meta's defense is that the glasses include a recording indicator light and that users are responsible for their own behavior. Alex Himel, who leads Meta's wearables business, told Dutch reporters before the hearing that the company has no plans to pull the glasses from the market. Hans Anders, one of the largest Dutch eyewear chains, had already suspended sales in the Netherlands and Belgium citing privacy concerns.

The case is the first courtroom test of whether AI-equipped wearables can be sold in Europe with their current default behavior, and it sits alongside enforcement moves from Italian, French and German regulators on the same product. A ruling in the Consumentenbond's favor would push every other AI-glasses maker — Snap, Google, Xreal, Apple on the roadmap — toward a Europe-only default where cameras stay off until an explicit user gesture. A ruling for Meta would signal that the EU-US baseline on wearable recording is settled at the device level, not the ecosystem level.

A note for learners: privacy law is not primarily about what a device can do — it is about what a device does by default, and who is responsible when the two drift apart. If you are designing a product that captures data about people who did not consent to be captured, assume the default will be what regulators scrutinize, not the toggle you ship behind a settings menu.
